strengths: The paper is technically well-grounded: it builds on the Adjoint Matching framework (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) and carefully extends it to a joint state-parameter evolution, which is a sensible and non-trivial extension for parameter-dependent PDE constraints where paired solution-parameter training data is unavailable.

The weak-form residual design is thoughtful: the Wendland–wavelet test function family with bridge mollifiers, normalisation against parameter-scaling degeneracy, and the explicit weak-form derivations for Darcy and wave equations are well executed and likely useful to practitioners.

The experimental coverage is broad relative to the method's scope: denoising, guidance from sparse parameter observations, 3D super-resolution with reflective boundaries, boundary misspecification, and an ablation of the parameter-space regularisation (λf, λx), including an appendix analysis showing that the λf = 0 variant exhibits mode collapse.
Reproducibility is addressed well: dataset generation, architectures, hyperparameters, runtimes, the full training algorithm, and a commitment to releasing dataset scripts are all documented.
The honest discussion of limitations (e.g., the acknowledged unfairness of the ECI comparison, blurrier acoustic parameter recovery due to architectural compromise) is a positive.
The paper is clearly written, with the method illustrated by a helpful figure and a sensible narrative connecting preference-based fine-tuning to physics-informed inference.
weaknesses: Limited novelty beyond applying Adjoint Matching: the core fine-tuning machinery is borrowed directly from Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025). The main new components — the surrogate base flow for α via the inverse predictor and the v_reg regularisation field — are heuristic and not theoretically justified. Once the running cost f ≠ 0 is introduced, the consistency of the fine-tuned distribution with the tilted target no longer holds, and the paper provides no analysis of what distribution the method actually targets.

Numerous empirical heuristics (geometric tail refinement of the time grid, computing the loss only over a subset of steps, loss clipping, normalisation of residuals by the parameter integral) depart substantially from the theory, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to these choices.

The experimental scope is narrow: only two canonical PDE systems with essentially binary parameter fields (a ∈ {3,12}, c ∈ {2,3}). Binary coefficients make the inverse problem considerably easier than the 'high-dimensional latent parameter' framing in the introduction suggests; no experiment with genuinely continuous, multi-scale parameter fields is presented.

Baselines are weak: there is no comparison against the most relevant prior methods that also enforce PDE constraints in generative models (e.g., Huang et al. 2024, Bastek et al. 2024, Baldan et al. 2025, Xu et al. 2025). The only head-to-head comparison is with ECI, which the authors themselves admit is unfair since it is gradient-free and PDE-oblivious.

For the inverse-problem claims, no evaluation of posterior calibration or uncertainty quantification is provided, despite the generative/Bayesian framing; only qualitative guided-sampling figures and pointwise diversity statistics are shown.

Claims that fine-tuning works 'without significantly affecting sample diversity' rely on custom pointwise MMSE/SMSE/diversity metrics; standard distributional measures or a comparison to a simple fine-tuning baseline (e.g., direct supervised fine-tuning on PDE-residual loss) are missing.

The guidance mechanism for sparse observations is standard classifier-style guidance applied to a learned quantity; the claim that this enables posterior sampling without paired data is supported only visually, without quantitative error metrics against ground-truth parameters.

Some experimental reporting is thin: e.g., Table 1/2/3 have few conditions, and error bars/number of runs (seeds) for the fine-tuning procedure are not reported, which matters given the acknowledged training instability (mode collapse without regularisation).

strengths: The paper is technically coherent and builds on a solid theoretical foundation (Adjoint Matching, Domingo-Enrich et al. 2025), recasting physics-constrained fine-tuning as stochastic optimal control.
The idea of jointly evolving latent physical parameters alongside the state is a sensible extension that enables inverse-problem inference without paired parameter–solution training data.

Weak-form residuals with randomly sampled compactly supported test functions are a well-motivated and numerically stable alternative to strong-form residuals, and the derivation details in Appendix C are thorough.

Reasonable ablations are provided: effect of the parameter regularization λf, fine-tuning strength λx, diversity/mode-collapse analysis (Table 2, Figs. 12–13, 17), and a qualitative comparison with ECI in Appendix E.

Implementation details, hyperparameters, runtimes, and a complete training algorithm (Algorithm 1) are given, and the authors commit to releasing dataset-generation scripts, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core machinery is directly borrowed from Adjoint Matching, with the reward simply replaced by a weak PDE residual. The main technical additions — a learned inverse predictor φ used to define surrogate base flows, and an ad hoc running cost f(α) that anchors fine-tuned parameters to base-model estimates — are engineering heuristics rather than principled contributions, and the λf regularizer lacks any theoretical justification.

Very narrow experimental scope: only two canonical PDE benchmarks (Darcy flow, acoustic wave), both with binary parameter fields taking values in {3,12} and {2,3}. These severely trivialize the inverse problem and undercut the central claim of solving 'ill-posed inverse problems' on 'high-dimensional' parameters; the motivating applications (weather, seismic, medical imaging) are never touched.

Weak baselines: no quantitative comparison against any of the closely related methods discussed at length in Related Work (Bastek et al., Huang et al./DiffusionPDE, Baldan et al./PBFM, Utkarsh et al., Zhang & Zou). The single comparison against ECI is acknowledged by the authors as 'not entirely fair' and is qualitative only. Consequently, it is impossible to judge whether the added complexity of fine-tuning is worth it over inference-time guidance/projection.

The authors themselves describe the experiments as 'preliminary', and the contribution list overpromises relative to what is delivered. Claims about uncertainty quantification, simulation-augmented discovery, and scientific discovery workflows are aspirational and untested.

The guidance mechanism for sparse observations is standard classifier-style guidance applied to the fine-tuned model, not a methodological contribution, and is evaluated only visually — no quantitative posterior accuracy, calibration, or coverage metrics are reported despite the framing in terms of Bayesian inverse problems.

Numerous undocumented deviations from the underlying theory (heuristic noise schedule modification with offset h, adaptive tail refinement of the time grid, loss clipping thresholds, computing the loss on only a fraction of time steps) weaken the theoretical grounding claimed in the contributions; the sensitivity of results to these choices is not analyzed.

Ablations are incomplete: the denoising result in Fig. 2 and the dependence on λx, λf are acknowledged by the authors to be hyperparameter-dependent, and only 20 samples are used for the acoustic evaluation, limiting statistical confidence.

Writing issues (e.g., 'pathalogical', inconsistent terminology around α/ω in figures and text, some figures referenced with incorrect numbering) and a relatively short, compressed experimental section further reduce polish.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned problem: post-training enforcement of parameter-dependent PDE constraints without paired parameter-solution data, which is distinct from most prior physics-constrained generative modeling that either trains with residuals from the start or assumes known coefficients.

The joint state-parameter flow construction is a sensible and non-trivial extension of Adjoint Matching: the surrogate base flow derived from a learned inverse predictor allows the framework to evolve latent parameters alongside solutions, and the regularization field toward base-model parameters gives a practical control-fidelity trade-off.

Use of weak-form residuals with randomly sampled compactly supported Wendland test functions is a sound engineering choice that avoids unstable high-order derivatives; the derivation and normalization details are thorough.
The scaled memoryless noise schedule (kappa) is a small but well-justified theoretical addition with a clean proof (Lemma 1), and it addresses a real numerical stability issue.

Comprehensive experimental suite: four PDE problems with deliberate model misspecification (BC changes, lossless assumption, removed forcing), observational noise, sparse-observation guidance, and a cross-domain image experiment. Extensive ablations (Base AM, Base AM+phi, PBFM, ECI), full hyperparameter tables, mis-specification sensitivity study (Fig. 13), and non-curated samples support the claims.

Lightweight and practical: fine-tuning requires only 20 gradient steps on Darcy (~15 minutes), and reported results show lower residuals than the base model with modest distributional shift, often dominating the ablation variants on the residual-MMD trade-off (notably MMD_alpha in Stokes and Helmholtz).

Strong reproducibility posture: detailed dataset generation, architecture tables, full training algorithm (Algorithm 1), loss computation heuristics, and a reproducibility statement with code promised.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method is essentially Adjoint Matching with (i) a PDE-residual reward, (ii) an augmented joint flow, and (iii) a trivially scaled noise schedule. Each component is a fairly natural combination of existing ideas; the theoretical contribution (Lemma 1) is minor. Reviewers may see this as incremental over Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025) plus PINF-style residuals.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat favorable by construction: PBFM is a training-time method that is inherently disadvantaged under deliberate misspecification, and ECI is only compared on one task. Stronger inference-time or post-training physics baselines (e.g., Utkarsh et al. 2025 guidance-style approaches, Christopher et al. 2024 projected diffusion) are discussed but not empirically compared.

Since the fine-tuning objective directly minimizes the weak residual, reduced weak residuals are partly guaranteed; the more meaningful evidence (strong residual and MMD) is reported but the margin over the cheaper Base AM ablations is sometimes small (e.g., Helmholtz weak residuals), and 'representative configurations' selected post hoc raise mild cherry-picking concerns despite the appendix containing full sweeps.

No quantitative evaluation of the inferred-parameter posterior quality (e.g., calibration, coverage, or comparison to ground-truth posterior samples); MMD_alpha alone does not establish that recovered parameters are statistically meaningful for inverse problems, which is a central claim of the paper.

No quantitative metrics for the natural-image experiment (PickScore values, FID, or user study); the recoloring demonstration remains purely qualitative and is a somewhat tenuous connection to the PDE-constrained setting.

Experiments are limited to 64x64 grids and ~20-25M parameter backbones; scalability of the joint flow and lean-adjoint procedure to 3D, multi-physics, or larger models (where the computational cost of adjoint ODE solves grows) is not demonstrated.

Several heuristic choices (surrogate one-step terminal parameter estimate, tilted time grid, loss clipping thresholds, step subsampling) are justified empirically rather than analyzed; sensitivity of results to these choices is not systematically studied.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important problem: enforcing parameter-dependent PDE constraints on pretrained generative models without paired (state, parameter) training data.

The proposed joint evolution of state and latent parameters via a surrogate base flow constructed from a learned inverse predictor is a sensible design, and the presentation of the method (Fig. 1, Algorithm 1) is reasonably detailed.

The theoretical observation that a scaled memoryless noise schedule σ²(t) = (1−κ)2η_t remains consistent (Lemma 1) is correct, and the appendix is thorough (test-function design, weak-form derivations, full hyperparameter tables).
Experiments span four PDE families plus a cross-domain image experiment, and the residual–distribution trade-off ablations (Figs. 3, 5, 7–11) are informative about the method's controllability.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core machinery is a fairly direct application of Adjoint Matching (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) with a weak-form PDE residual as the reward. Weak-form PINN-style losses and reward fine-tuning are both well established; the 'novel extension' claimed (a scalar κ scaling of the noise schedule) is a one-line lemma and is oversold. The inverse-predictor surrogate flow is a reasonable but engineering-level addition rather than a conceptual advance.

The central claim of 'accurate recovery of latent coefficients' (abstract) is not supported. No experiment reports parameter-recovery accuracy against ground-truth α; evaluation relies only on MMD and residual metrics, which can be low even when the inferred parameters are wrong (the ill-posedness of the inverse problem is precisely the concern). This is a serious gap between claims and evidence.

Baseline comparisons are weak and potentially unfair. PBFM is augmented with the authors' own inverse predictor and evaluated on deliberately misspecified settings that 'naturally place them at a disadvantage' (App. E.2); no comparison to strong guidance/posterior-sampling baselines (e.g., DiffusionPDE-style guidance on a jointly pretrained model, or Bayesian posterior samplers) is given. Several ablation rows (Tables 10–13) show Base AM variants matching or beating the full method on some metrics, and headline tables cherry-pick 'representative configurations' selected by the best metric.

Improvements over the base model are often modest and mixed. E.g., in Darcy the strong residual improves only from 7.1e1 to ~4.7e1 while MMDx degrades substantially as the reward weight increases; the reported gains in Helmholtz and Stokes are largely on MMDα, with residual levels similar across all AM variants (as the authors themselves note in Sec. 4.5).

The natural-image experiment is only qualitative (a single curated prompt, two classes, no quantitative metrics) and serves mainly to demonstrate that the framework reduces to PickScore-based fine-tuning; it does not validate the physics-inference claims and feels tangential.

The ill-posedness of the joint inverse problem is not analyzed: when the mapping x → α is non-unique (as in Darcy with piecewise-constant permeability), nothing prevents the fine-tuned model from collapsing to an arbitrary parameter branch, and the λ_f regularization is only empirically motivated. No discussion of identifiability, uncertainty, or failure modes.

Clarity and polish issues: several awkward or garbled formulations (e.g., Eq. 1's coefficient combination, stray symbols in appendices), inconsistent error-bar semantics (MSE entries like 1.71e-6 ± 0.50 in Table 1), and a dense, hard-to-parse Figure 1. Data-generation scripts are only 'promised' rather than released, weakening reproducibility of the synthetic benchmarks.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important problem: enforcing parameter-dependent PDE constraints on generative models when the parameters are unobserved, i.e., without paired parameter–solution training data. This is a meaningful gap relative to prior physics-constrained diffusion/FM work (Bastek et al., PBFM, DiffusionPDE, projection methods), which either require joint data, training-time physics losses, or hard constraints.

The method is theoretically grounded rather than ad hoc: it reformulates fine-tuning as stochastic optimal control via the Adjoint Matching framework, and the extension to a joint (state, parameter) flow with a surrogate base parameter flow derived from a pretrained inverse predictor is a principled construction. The scaled memoryless noise schedule (κ) extension is simple but is actually proven consistent (Lemma 1 in App. D.4), which is a nice touch.

The experimental program is unusually thorough for this area: four distinct PDE families (Darcy, elasticity, Helmholtz, Stokes) with deliberately introduced misspecifications (boundary mismatch, damped-vs-lossless, forcing mismatch), plus a cross-domain natural-image experiment; weak/strong residuals, MMD metrics, SSIM-based diversity, and full hyperparameter sweeps relegated to extensive appendix tables (Tables 10-13).

Sensible ablation design: Base AM and Base AM+φ variants cleanly isolate the contribution of the joint parameter flow, and the λx/λα/λf sweeps illustrate an interpretable residual-vs-fidelity trade-off (Fig. 3, Fig. 5). The Stokes result that only the joint model reaches the low-MMDα regime is a concrete, well-supported claim.

Practicality is demonstrated: fine-tuning is lightweight (20 gradient steps / <15 minutes for Darcy on a single L40S), and sampling proceeds at base-model cost with no inference-time modification — a real advantage over inference-time projection/guidance methods.
The appendix is comprehensive (dataset generation details, weak-form derivations per PDE, test-function design, full training algorithm), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental. The backbone is Adjoint Matching (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) applied with a PDE-residual reward; the main extensions — a joint parameter flow built on a pretrained inverse predictor, a scaled memoryless schedule, and a regularization running cost — are reasonable but modest contributions relative to the claimed 'framework' framing.

Results gains are sometimes marginal. In Helmholtz (Table 2), the joint model reduces weak residual from 4.9 (Base AM) to 4.3 and strong residual from ~1.3×10^1 to ~1.05×10^1 — improvements that are modest and come with wide error bars; in Stokes the attainable weak residuals of all AM variants are explicitly similar, with the advantage confined to MMDα.

Evaluation lacks direct parameter-recovery accuracy against ground truth. The abstract claims 'accurate recovery of latent coefficients', but results are measured via residuals and MMD against a synthetic reference set Dref, not against true α fields; a quantitative posterior/estimation error analysis (e.g., CRPS or RMSE vs. ground truth, as in Bayesian inverse problem benchmarks) is missing.
The guidance-on-sparse-observations experiment (Sec. 4.2) is purely qualitative with no quantitative conditioning-error metric, weakening the inverse-problem claims for that setting.

Introducing the running state cost f(α) for regularization departs from the f=0 setting under which the adjoint-matching consistency guarantee holds; the paper does not analyze what distribution the fine-tuned model targets when f≠0, so the theoretical guarantee claimed for the full method (not just the κ-scaled schedule) is unclear.

The natural-image experiment (parametric recoloring via PickScore) is a loose analogy to the physics setting and provides only qualitative samples on one or two classes; it is a toy demonstration rather than strong evidence of cross-domain utility.

All PDE evaluation is on small synthetic 64×64 datasets generated by the authors; no comparison to existing published benchmarks or to inference-time guidance approaches like DiffusionPDE quantitatively. Some presentation issues also exist (e.g., Table 1 referenced as 'Table 4.3', PBFM's failed convergence on Stokes limits the baseline comparison there).
